name: Carlos Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills your working days?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Carlos, 43, and have a master’s in music. I lead the brass section of a regional theatre band, record short trumpet cues, timed musical passages, for local programmes and teach six intermediate pupils. I can keep a section together when a show changes tempo, though leading is more listening than showing off. I like hearing a new player land an entrance; I dislike finding that a copied cue was used twice for one fee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work fit your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works regular hours at a public library, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My music pay is about typical, with three months of expenses saved and some similar jobs nearby. I have never used AI; I mark up printed music and phone the stage manager when a date changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band that faster ticket emails are fine if the theatre still pays for rehearsal time. A trumpet player has to hear the actor, not just the computer clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our three-month reserve and my partner’s library pay can cover one delayed show fee. The mortgage is steady for now, although I would ask about any reuse of an old trumpet recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the booked theatre shows and six pupils this term. This week I’d ask for the next paid rehearsal dates and cue-reuse terms in writing, then save a fifth of each cleared cue fee after household bills are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few months in this mild version. One late invoice is irritating, but it would not stop the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was a cue reused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A director played last season’s trumpet opening at a new event without calling me. I asked for the agreed reuse fee before recording another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let a tool print the music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool. I would read the printed part and play it before giving it to another musician.

I would ask for written **cue-reuse terms** before another recording.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and library wage cover one late fee.
A reused **trumpet cue** can still cost me a payment.
do: Keep **theatre shows** and six pupils this term.
Confirm **rehearsal dates** and reuse terms; save one fifth of cleared cue fees after bills.
feel: I feel **calm** because current pay and savings cover one delay.
S0.quote: A trumpet player has to hear the actor, not just the computer clock.
fieldNote: His **senior skill** does not mean unusually high pay; it supports regular theatre leadership.
He **never uses AI** and checks written parts by playing them.

steps.text: Keep booked theatre shows and six paid pupils this term
Save fifth of each cleared cue fee after mortgage and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that generated trumpet cues and schedules will arrive before a robot can join the band. I would ask for paid rehearsal and recording terms before handing over another file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The short cues and part preparation make about a quarter of my music pay. If the theatre buys generated parts instead, we can manage a few months, but the lost fees will slow mortgage saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d bring my last season’s cue invoices to the theatre manager and ask for a written minimum rehearsal and reuse fee. In the first year, if cue orders fall, I’d stop hiring the separate recording booth on days without a paying session and keep my six pupils and live shows while booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a real cut to my own fees. Three months saved helps us choose, but losing a quarter of my pay every term still changes our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a generated trumpet part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and would not upload a pupil’s playing to experiment. I would ask to see a printed part and check every note on my trumpet before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager refuses a minimum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two other local bands for their posted rates, then decide whether to apply. I would not leave a paid show for a rumour.

I would say **generated cues** threaten recording pay before live playing.
think: Cues and preparation make about **one quarter** of music pay.
The **three-month reserve** cannot cover that gap year after year.
do: Bring **cue invoices** to the manager this month for written minimum and reuse fees.
Stop **booth hire** on empty days if orders fall; keep paid shows and pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a recurring cut to my own fee income.
S1.quote: Three months saved helps us choose, but losing a quarter of my pay every term still changes our plans.
fieldNote: His **recording exposure** is a quarter of pay despite live section leadership and a three-month household reserve.
He avoids **AI tools** and protects paid work through direct contract terms.

steps.text: Ask theatre manager for written minimum rehearsal and cue-reuse fees using invoices

Keep six paid pupils and live theatre shows while booked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band that thinking AGI by 2028 could write trumpet cues and rehearsal plans, while robots that play hands-on parts follow around 2031. I would ask for signed live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the short cue fees to stop in 2028, and the theatre might cut paid preparation too. Three months saved gives us a short search, but losing a quarter of pay would still bite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d get the theatre’s paid calls and pupils’ next term in writing. In the first year after AGI arrives, if cue and preparation fees fall, I’d end the separate booth rental at renewal and apply for an advertised paid school band-leader role only if the school accepts my master’s and experience and written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees with school pickup covered; I’d keep theatre work and six pupils until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, because I can act but cannot carry a permanent pay cut on three months saved. I need a school wage that replaces trumpet fees, not another unpaid title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept an unpaid trial lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the school how I teach during a paid audition or a short observed lesson. I would not give up a theatre call for a free week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can your partner collect the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can collect on most library days, but the late shift changes that. I would confirm the actual rota or paid childcare before accepting school hours.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from robot players around 2031.
I would ask for **signed live dates** before counting theatre income.
think: I expect **cue fees** to end and preparation may shrink.
Our **three-month reserve** buys search time, not lasting wage replacement.
do: Keep **theatre and pupils** until signed school offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
End **booth rental** at renewal if 2028 cue and preparation fees fall.
Seek posted paid **school band-leader work** after cue/preparation loss: degree/experience accepted, written replacement net-after-travel pay, pickup or childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a real quarter-pay loss despite some options.
S2.quote: I need a school wage that replaces trumpet fees, not another unpaid title.
fieldNote: Thinking AGI threatens **cue writing** before robot trumpet players arrive around 2031.
A school move needs **actual opening**, accepted credentials, written replacement pay and confirmed pickup or childcare.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre dates and six pupils until signed school offer
End separate booth rental at renewal if 2028 cue/preparation fees fall
Seek advertised paid school band-leader role after cue/preparation loss; degree/experience accepted, replacement written net-after-travel pay, pickup/childcare
Use paid auditions/short observed lessons; keep theatre calls instead of a free teaching week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the town’s players that five years is time to prove a live brass workshop earns a fee. Thinking AGI could take cue writing around 2031 before capable robot trumpeters arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could replace some cue income by teaching adults to play together, but a free room alone will not pay an assistant. I will not take money from the mortgage reserve to make a class look busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask an independent arts hall for a room without a deposit and invite nine adults to prepay for five Saturday brass sessions. I’d start only if the money covers my teaching and preparation, a paid assistant’s setup and teaching, safe loan instruments and confirmed child pickup; in the first year after 2031 I’d repeat only if nine still pay those costs, the room stays free and pickup holds, while keeping paid theatre dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about cue fees going before the group proves itself. We have a few months saved, but an empty workshop still sends the mortgage bill home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you check the borrowed instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall has some old trumpets, and I would ask a qualified repairer to check their valves and mouthpieces before anyone pays a deposit. If safe instruments are not ready, I would postpone the class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only six adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund the six and keep my current pupils. Six fees would not cover two teachers and safe instruments without using family savings.

I would offer a **paid brass workshop** only with enough real adults.
think: Nine **prepaid adults** might replace cue fees only if both teachers earn.
A **free room** does not pay the assistant or repair unsafe instruments.
do: Start **brass workshop** with free room, nine prepayments covering my teaching/prep, assistant setup/teaching, repairer-checked instruments and pickup.
Repeat the **workshop** after 2031 only if nine cover all costs, room free and pickup confirmed; keep theatre dates.
feel: I feel **anxious** about cue loss while testing a paid workshop.
S3.quote: I could replace some cue income by teaching adults to play together, but a free room alone will not pay an assistant.
fieldNote: His **independent workshop** needs nine prepayments covering both teachers and safe loan instruments.

Repeat after 2031 if nine cover teachers/prep/setup, instruments safe, room free and pickup confirmed
Keep paid theatre dates and six pupils while booked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that a decade is enough time to learn an instrument and ask what a rehearsal actually pays. Thinking AGI arrives around 2036, and robot trumpeters follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still lead theatre brass, but recording fees may be smaller by then. Our three-month reserve and my partner’s library wage make the next few years manageable if paid shows continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep theatre dates and six pupils and save a fifth of each cleared extra cue fee after mortgage and food toward six months of expenses. Over the decade I’d offer the brass workshop only with a free room, nine prepayments covering my teaching and preparation, the assistant’s setup and teaching, safe checked trumpets, and confirmed pickup; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep it only while those fees cover us and apply for an advertised school band role if cue pay ends, provided my master’s qualifies and the written net offer after travel replaces lost pay with pickup covered, while retaining current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant recording market, not this month’s food bill. I can save a little when an extra cue actually pays, but I cannot write tomorrow’s fee into today’s account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy instruments for a future group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would use the hall’s safe loan trumpets only after a qualified check and before taking deposits. The mortgage reserve is not a shop account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school offers only a volunteer title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep playing and teaching for pay. I would move only for a posted offer with hours and net pay in writing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue fees could stop before I see a school offer, and three months saved will not last through a long search. Signed theatre dates, an actual school vacancy with net pay replacing lost fees, and a workshop that pays both teachers would help. I will not fill a hall by borrowing from the mortgage account.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the borrowed trumpets before a child tries one. An old instrument may look fine on a shelf and still be unsafe to play.

headlineQuote: An old instrument may look fine on a shelf and still be unsafe to play.
portrait: Carlos is a **43-year-old brass leader** with a music master’s, theatre work, cue recordings and six pupils.
His **typical pay**, library-employed partner, mortgage and three-month reserve support two school-age children.
He **never uses AI** and protects live fees through direct contracts and a safe, prepaid workshop.
Fast AGI threatens **cue income** before robot trumpeters; he considers a real school opening only with replacement pay.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could end cue pay before a viable school offer.
whatWouldHelp: Signed **theatre dates** and a posted school vacancy with replacement net pay would help.
Nine **prepaid adults** covering both teachers and safe instruments would support a separate workshop.
